components.text: Religion merely appropriates prior human goodness while adding corrupting doctrine and institutional power.
Christianity must identify a distinct good rather than merely internal criticism of religious corruption.
Whether religion merely adds poison rather than containing resources that criticize corrupt religious power.
Whether a distinctively Christian principle supplies an identifiable good capable of meeting the proposed test.
Identify a uniquely religious good that is not merely an independently human contribution.
Compassion and service arise prior to religion and are only appropriated by it.
Whether Christianity supplied a distinctively religious good through neighbor-directed devotion and humanitarian institutions.
Whether compassion is exhaustively prior and human rather than historically shaped by Christian devotion.
Religion is the distinctive source of poison added to otherwise prior human decency.
A successful reply must show a uniquely religious good unaccompanied by religious harm.
Whether violence and domination are distinctively introduced by religion or are a general human problem.
Whether Christianity's cruciform antidote constitutes a uniquely good contribution without accompanying harm.
Christian community and charity constitute extraordinary religious goods and institutional fruits.
Internal religious criticism distinguishes authentic blessing from corrupt religious power.
The primary poison is generally human rather than distinctively religious.
Whether religious community and charity count as unqualified goods once accompanying doctrinal harms are included.
Whether identified harms can be assigned to religious doctrine rather than only general human vice.
Christian devotion generated a distinct compassion revolution and associated institutions.
Christianity supplies a distinct antidote to generally human pride and violence.
Whether community is a uniquely religious contribution rather than a reproducible human social good.
Whether Christianity's proposed antidote supplies a distinctive contribution beyond ordinary human community.
Christianity generated major humanitarian institutions and reforms from its distinctive devotion.
Christian standards can criticize corrupt religious power from within the tradition.
Christianity functions as an antidote to general human domination and violence.
Whether claimed Christian humanitarian causation withstands the prolonged record of Christian institutional power over slavery.
Whether Christian standards functioned as an effective antidote when Christian authorities possessed governing power.
Humanity supplies an unpoisoned well of decency before religion adds pride, violence, and domination.
Religion fails unless it supplies unique good without introducing any bad.
Christian political dominance had adequate capacity yet failed to prohibit slavery.
The premise that religion arrives after an otherwise unpoisoned stock of human decency and adds the relevant brutality.
The demand for a uniquely religious good with no accompanying bad consequence.
The historical claim that Christian political power failed to abolish slavery categorically.
Religious doctrines accompanying community subordinate women and impose serious social harms.
Humane benefits are prior human goods rather than distinctively religious contributions.
A religious principle must supply a unique good without an accompanying bad.
Whether Christian sexual doctrine only subordinates women or also materially constrains exploitative male power.
Whether Christianity supplies a distinctive institutional mechanism protecting women and children.
Christian doctrine protects and elevates women by constraining elite male sexual access.
Christian scripture and devotion generate compassionate institutions and practices.
Christianity contains internal standards that criticize corrupt or oppressive religious power.
The inference that a humane presentation of Christian sexual ethics derives its protective character from explicit scriptural teaching.
The claim that Christian compassion is generated by scripture and devotion rather than imported human concern.
The claim that internal Christian standards adequately correct harmful explicit teachings.
Christian authorities lacked or failed to articulate a categorical doctrinal basis for rejecting human ownership.
Moral opposition to domination is an independently human good appropriated by religion.
Humane Christian reform must retreat from scripture and import external compassion.
Whether Christianity supplies a doctrinal reason that categorically condemns enslaving human beings.
Whether equal human status has a distinctively Christian doctrinal foundation.
Whether the humane antislavery principle is drawn from scripture rather than imported from outside it.
Christian compassion is imported from outside scripture and doctrine rather than grounded within Christianity.
Love and compassion are wholly prior human goods merely appropriated by religion.
Christian institutions failed historically to prohibit slavery despite their power.
The premise that Christian appeals to love and goodness necessarily abandon doctrine or import an external humane standard.
Whether love and goodness possess a specifically Christian theological foundation rather than being merely appropriated human goods.
Christian political dominance could have prohibited slavery but instead tolerated human ownership for centuries.
Humane reform succeeds only by moving away from explicit biblical doctrine.
Equality and reforming concern arise independently of Christian doctrine.
Why Christian teaching did not immediately prohibit slavery despite affirming equality and possessing institutional influence.
Whether antislavery equality can be derived from Pauline and Christian doctrine itself.
Christianity necessarily transformed slavery gradually because its movement works socially like yeast.
Christian institutions achieved radical reforms such as opposition to infanticide.
Image-of-God doctrine supplied an abolitionist basis against slavery.
The premise that Christianity's gradual method explains its failure to abolish slavery promptly.
The claimed ability of Christian institutions to enact major humanitarian changes such as ending infanticide.
The claim that Christian anthropology supplied a sufficiently operative antislavery principle.
Community and compassion are ordinary human goods reproducible without religion.
Compassion and love are wholly prior human goods merely claimed by religion.
Christianity must identify a uniquely religious moral contribution.
Whether universalized concern for enemies and the weak is simply ordinary prior human decency.
Whether Christianity contributes only generic community rather than an unusually expansive moral norm.
Whether love of enemies constitutes a uniquely Christian good with no accompanying religious harm.
God's eternal loving nature grounds goodness and avoids arbitrary divine-command morality.
Divine image-bearing provides a stable Christian foundation for equal human worth.
Christianity authoritatively extends love to enemies, outsiders, and the weak.
Whether identifying goodness with God's loving nature can morally constrain commands attributed to God.
Whether sacred human status consistently prohibits grave violence against divine image-bearers.
Whether Christian enemy love coheres with divinely commanded conquest narratives.
Shared moral recognition of atrocity is sufficient to test claims that divine commands express goodness.
Human decency supplies moral standards prior to and independently of religion.
Historical delay undermines Christianity's claimed moral authority concerning slavery.
Whether the affirmative can condemn conquest and slavery objectively without a ground beyond present agreement.
Whether shared human decency supplies an objective rather than contingent moral foundation.
Whether later moral condemnation establishes objective improvement rather than changed social preference.
Christianity uniquely scaled morally valuable concern beyond ordinary kin and tribal boundaries.
Modern compassion and institutions are distinctively derivative of Christianity.
Objective moral condemnation requires a foundation beyond contingent human agreement.
The premise that socially valuable compassion and family practices require distinctively Christian derivation.
The claim that major modern moral goods are uniquely generated by Christian devotion and institutions.
The separate question whether non-Christian moral goods possess an objective metaethical foundation.
The conquest commands apparently authorize indiscriminate atrocity and contradict God's loving nature.
Humane Christian interpretation retreats from explicit scripture toward external compassion.
Christian moral claims require comparison with independent non-Christian contributions.
Whether the conquest narratives straightforwardly command the indiscriminate atrocities used to challenge divine goodness.
Whether Christian nonviolence is a doctrinal culmination rather than a retreat from scripture.
Whether Christianity contains an authoritative prohibition on religious violence.
Judgment on a violent child-sacrificing culture and ancient context morally explain the conquest commands.
Divine goodness is identical with eternal love and cannot be arbitrary command.
Christianity makes concern for enemies and the weak morally authoritative.
The inference that judgment for child sacrifice can morally justify killing the judged population's children.
Whether the conquest defense remains consistent with identifying divine goodness as love.
Whether internal Christian standards successfully criticize the apparent religious violence in this case.
